summary: This program models basic houseplant care with four functions, each showing a different return type: one that returns nothing, one that returns a boolean, one an int, and one a String. The main method calls each in turn and prints the values that come back.

lines.text: This call stands alone as its own statement because plantInSoil() hands nothing back — trying to wrap it in a println would be an error, since there is no value to print.
The other three calls sit inside println because each one produces a value; the call is replaced by whatever the function returns before the message is joined together and printed.
A return type of void declares complete emptiness — the function does its work by printing and sends nothing back to the caller.
Once a function declares a return type other than void, it must actually return a value of that type; boolean here means the return statement has to supply true or false.
waterLevel() returns the int 3, and Java converts that number to text automatically when the + joins it to the message in main.
Reference types such as String can be returned just as easily as primitives, so a function is free to hand back a whole message rather than a single number or flag.
